meta.title: Crochet Plushie Business Dashboard
meta.notes: Source data compiled via research through July 2026. Re-verify time-sensitive figures (postage rates, platform pricing, unconfirmed convention dates) periodically.
changelog: Convention cost/barrier-to-entry data added 2026-07-10 via vendor-page research -- many table costs are gated behind an application step and could not be confirmed publicly; re-verify directly with organizers before budgeting.

Product-demand research (bestsellers, price clustering, bundling, under-represented items) added 2026-07-10 -- mostly craft-business blog consensus rather than raw sales data; several items are flagged as single-source or outright data gaps.

Added Chico Renaissance and Fantasy Faire 2026-07-11. Corrected 2026-07-11: initial 'inaugural event' framing was based on one source without cross-checking -- sources actually conflict on its history (see its note). A related but distinct event, Golden Goblet Faire (formerly Chico Renaissance Faire, founded 2025), was found during that cross-check and confirmed discontinued -- not added as a bookable convention since it can no longer be applied to.
Removed the Premium Features page 2026-07-11 (removable-parts pricing research and Wix platform pricing comparison) at the owner's request.
Deduplicated 2026-07-11: the email-list finding in Booth Presentation was a full duplicate of the dedicated Email List Building & Usage section -- replaced with a cross-reference pointer.

Merged 2026-07-11: mystery/grab-bag research existed on both the Clearance and Product Demand pages -- consolidated onto Clearance (with the Etsy bundling-ratio and TikTok-trend details folded in) and replaced the Product Demand entries with a cross-reference.
Added At-a-Glance synthesis bullets to the three research pages 2026-07-11 -- editorial takeaways derived from existing findings, labeled as synthesis rather than sourced research.

Expanded event coverage 2026-07-11 with a second research pass: added CA ren faires (Valhalla, Calaveras Celtic, Folsom, Kearney), oddities/horror markets (Oddities & Curiosities Expo, Midsummer Scream, Menagerie, Witching Hour), craft/holiday shows (Crocker, Harvest Festival, Renegade SF, Maker Faire, Chico Christmas Faire, Your Local Marketplace), and smaller fandom events (Further Confusion, Sac Gamers Expo, Anime Destiny, NorCal Cherry Blossom Festival). Confirmed defunct, do not chase: Koroneburg Old World Festival, ScareLA, J-Pop Summit, Crunchyroll Expo, Silicon Valley Comic Con, Kraken Con; NorCal Pirate Festival is venue-less/watch-list only.

conventions.name: Chico Renaissance and Fantasy Faire
conventions.note: Free entry, community/family-oriented, run by Your Local Marketplace + the nonprofit Sound Source. Theme is 'radical inclusivity' welcoming knights, fairies, dragons, vampires, wizards and witches. Marketplace features 80+ small businesses/local artists. CONFLICTING SOURCES on history: the event's own copy on butte365.com calls it 'the inaugural Chico Renaissance and Fantasy Faire' (first year under this name/organizer), but a different page on the organizer's own site says it 'returns to' Patrick Ranch Museum. Likely explanation: an earlier, differently-named 'Chico Renaissance Faire' rebranded to 'Golden Goblet Faire' (founded 2025) -- which is now confirmed DISCONTINUED per its own site ('this fair is no longer active,' per The Renlist directory). This Sept 2026 event appears to be a fresh, unrelated relaunch by a different organizer, not a continuation of Golden Goblet Faire -- but treat the 'inaugural' framing as unconfirmed rather than certain.

clearingOldInventory.howItWorks: Bundle unsold/overstock pieces into a sealed surprise bag
clearingOldInventory.note: Repeatedly described as 'always a best seller' on TikTok -- documented as effective specifically in this market, not just generic advice Well-established as an actively sold format on Etsy specifically for crochet plushies, typically bundling 2-3 plushies to meet or exceed the paid value (Etsy mystery bag market listings, confidence: Medium). Popularity may be partly tied to TikTok 'gacha'/'lucky box' trends rather than pure value-seeking (inferred from Etsy listing tags, confidence: Low).

clearingOldInventory.howItWorks: Same as above but themed rather than fully random
clearingOldInventory.note: Real precedent: a 'horror mystery bag' (mini Freddy/Michael/Jason figures) marketed with #comiccon tags. Directly applicable to a Cryptid Mystery Bag sold at Sinister Creature Con / Sinister Halloween Con.
Frequent discounting erodes perceived value and trains customers to wait for sales

clearingOldInventory.howItWorks: Pair a slow mover with a popular item at a bundled discount
clearingOldInventory.note: Frames as 'more for less' rather than 'this didn't sell'

clearingOldInventory.howItWorks: Pick specific items each week for an extra discount instead of a blanket clearance sale
clearingOldInventory.note: Avoids the psychological 'clearance' framing that can devalue the brand

clearingOldInventory.howItWorks: Show original price crossed out next to discounted price
clearingOldInventory.note: Makes the discount feel more substantial

copyrightNotes.lovecraftSpecific: Most Lovecraft stories are public domain in the US (never renewed, or pre-1929). The Cthulhu Mythos was an intentionally 'open' shared universe from the start. Generic tentacled elder-god designs based on text descriptions are safe; copying a specific illustrator's or game company's distinctive rendering is not.
copyrightNotes.riskEvidence: 2019 Baby Yoda craze produced real Disney cease-and-desist letters to crochet pattern bloggers -- concrete evidence recognizable-IP risk is not theoretical.

conventionRankings.caveat: Most convention vendor pricing is gated behind an application step rather than posted publicly, even for major events (Anime Expo, SDCC, WonderCon, L.A. Comic Con). Treat "not publicly posted" entries as needing direct outreach before budgeting.

bestsellers.finding: Small/quick amigurumi under ~4in (mushrooms, mini bears, strawberries, ghosts, donuts) consistently outsell larger, detailed pieces at in-person events -- shoppers buy them on impulse.
Keychains/mini charms are fast-selling, low-yarn, low-risk items that often serve as a booth 'entry point' drawing buyers in before bigger purchases.
Animal designs (octopus, axolotl, cats, dogs, bears, turtles) and food-shaped items are named most often as reliable bestsellers, ahead of niche fandom pieces.
Medium-size plushies ($20-$50) are the format kids gravitate to for play value (e.g. snuggle dragons), distinct from keychains bought as impulse/gift items.
Sellers explicitly prioritize fast-to-make items over highly detailed pieces for craft-fair viability -- a supply-side signal (seller convenience), not direct proof of lower demand for large pieces.

priceRange.finding: $10-$25 is repeatedly identified as the core impulse-buy range at craft fairs/conventions for keychains, small plushies, and similar giftable items.
One source frames $25-$50 (not $20) as where most sales likely live, reserving $10-$20 for the smallest impulse items only.
Two-tier pricing pattern reported: mini amigurumi/keychains cluster at $8-$18; medium plushies with safety eyes cluster at $20-$35.
'$20 and under' is explicitly and repeatedly used as vendor shorthand for the psychological impulse-buy threshold, though no hard sales data was cited by any source.
New/beginner vendors are advised to start at $5-$10/item before working up to a $20-25/hour-of-labor pricing target used by more experienced sellers.

bundles.finding: '3 for $X' bundle pricing (e.g. 3-for-$18, 3-for-$25) is recommended across multiple sources as a way to move small plushies/keychains faster and pair slow movers with bestsellers.
'Buy 2 get 1 free' deals are cited as a top performer by one vendor account -- but in jewelry, not plushies, so treat as an adjacent-craft signal only.

Mystery/grab bags are a well-established bundling format for crochet plushies -- see the Clearing Old Inventory page for pricing, the horror-mystery-bag precedent, and TikTok-trend context (merged there to avoid duplicating the same research on two pages).
No source quantifies bundling as a percentage of total sales for finished plushies -- only qualitative "bundles increase average transaction size" claims exist.

gaps.finding: Skin-tone yarn availability is a documented pain point among crafters, prompting creation of a dedicated 8-shade skin-tone yarn line -- maker-side evidence is stronger than confirmed end-customer demand.
Custom/made-to-order plushies show demand signals via active seller waitlists (explicit 'There is a Waitlist!' listings), suggesting custom capacity is a bottleneck for at least some shops.
Allergen/hypoallergenic material guidance appears mainly as seller-side safety advice, not documented buyer complaints -- currently a data gap, not a confirmed underserved niche.
No direct evidence found on size-option gaps, LGBTQ+ representation, or adult/collector positioning via Reddit/TikTok searches -- flagged as a genuine research gap, not a "no demand" finding.
gaps.source: N/A -- recommend a manual Reddit/TikTok search pass if decision-critical

atAGlance: Stock small: under-4in minis and keychains in the $10-$25 impulse range are the proven engine; medium plushies ($20-$35) serve kids and gift buyers.
Two proven multi-item formats: '3 for $X' bundles and mystery/grab bags (detail on the Clearance page).
The '$20 and under' impulse threshold is vendor consensus, not hard data -- one source argues $25-$50 is where most revenue actually lives.
Best-documented gaps to exploit: skin-tone yarn availability and made-to-order capacity (waitlists signal unmet demand).
Weakest evidence: no one quantifies bundle share of sales, and large statement pieces are under-tested rather than disproven.

yarnBrands.finding: Chenille/blanket-style yarn is the dominant category for sellable plushies; in a 7-yarn side-by-side maker test, Hobbii Baby Snuggle rated softest and easiest to work with, while Bernat Blanket rated firmest (best for shape retention).

Premier Parfait Chunky and Hobbii Baby Snuggle are treated as near-interchangeable substitutes by plushie makers on TikTok (same thickness, overlapping colors) -- useful backup when one is out of stock.

Among standard acrylics, Red Heart Super Saver (cheapest, widest colors, scratchy), Caron Simply Soft (softer but splitty), and Hobby Lobby I Love This Yarn recur most in Reddit comparisons -- consensus is all three work and choice is preference-driven.
WeCrochet/Knit Picks Brava (worsted/sport) is a frequently blogged best-value amigurumi acrylic: soft, durable, machine-washable, huge palette including skin tones, ~$2.49-2.99/skein.
For cotton, Paintbox Cotton DK (~$2-3/skein, big palette) appears in best-amigurumi-yarn roundups; no strong amigurumi-specific ranking found for Lion Brand 24/7 Cotton or Scheepjes Catona.

yarnPricing.finding: Bernat Blanket (10.5oz/220yd): Walmart 6-pack listed at $19.99 (~$3.33/skein, ~1.5 cents/yd) but other Walmart listings show ~$9.50/skein -- pricing varies wildly by listing; multipacks are generally the cheapest route. Verify at checkout.
Premier Parfait Chunky (3.5oz/131yd): $5.49/skein direct from Premier (~4.2 cents/yd); Michaels marketplace listings run $9.78-14.34 -- buy direct or Walmart, not Michaels marketplace.
Hobbii Honey Bunny: $9.60/skein at 1-3 units with quantity discounts at higher counts; Hobbii Baby Snuggle ~$8.80/skein (2024 observation).
WeCrochet Brava Worsted: $2.49/skein for 218yd (~1.1 cents/yd) -- among the cheapest quality acrylics available.

Joann is gone: all ~790 stores liquidated by May 30, 2025. Michaels acquired Joann's IP and private labels (e.g. Big Twist). Practical channels now: Michaels, Hobby Lobby, Walmart, and direct online (Yarnspirations, Hobbii, Crochet.com).

qualityReputation.finding: Bernat Blanket (current yarn): praised for firmness/shape retention, but documented complaints of skein-to-skein color-run and tension inconsistency even within the same dye lot, plus a long official discontinued-shades list (9 standard + 58 Blanket Big) -- a real color-continuity risk for a fixed product line.

Chenille/velvet yarns generally (incl. Bernat Velvet): worming (loops popping out of finished fabric) and shedding are the most-cited issues; standard fix is smaller hooks and tighter tension. Yarn ends are prone to wiggling loose in amigurumi.
Caron Simply Soft is frequently criticized for splitting during tight amigurumi stitches; Red Heart Super Saver is durable and cheap but scratchy for a premium plushie feel.
Hobbii Baby Snuggle/Honey Bunny praised as softest with strong cores; one maker warns Hobbii's newer 'Toucan' chenille has a weaker inner thread (single-source anecdote).
WeCrochet Brava reviewers report it 'never feels cheap' with good stitch definition and durability -- few complaints found.

bulkWholesale.finding: Yarnspirations has a formal wholesale program (contact form) plus retail tiered promos ('Buy 3-4, get 10% off') and clearance up to 60% -- the most direct wholesale path for Bernat Blanket.
Hobbii has no published wholesale program but offers built-in quantity discounts (e.g. Honey Bunny cheaper at 4+ skeins), color-pack bundles, 50%-off sale collections, and free US shipping at $75+.
Walmart multipacks (6- and 10-pack Bernat Blanket) are effectively the cheapest bulk channel without a wholesale account, though listing prices are inconsistent.
WeCrochet Brava functions as a de facto bulk value line (~1.1 cents/yd retail, no minimums). True wholesale minimum-order details for Hobbii or LoveCrafts: not found.

eyesAndStuffing.finding: 6060eyes.com (18+ year amigurumi specialist) sells bulk safety-eye packs (e.g. 25 pairs of 6mm solid black, typical small packs ~$1.50-2.85), US child-safety compliant. Note: their Etsy store was suspended March 2024 -- they now sell only via their own site.
GlassEyesOnline is a wholesale-oriented supplier of safety eyes/noses in all sizes (listings from ~$6) -- good for odd sizes and animal noses.

Fairfield Poly-Fil Premium 10lb box is the standard business-scale stuffing; reviewers cite Walmart as ~20% cheaper than other channels (eBay listing ~$74.70, 2025-26; Walmart typically notably less -- exact current price unconfirmed).

atAGlance: Chenille rules sellable plushies: Bernat Blanket (current yarn) is firmest for shape retention, Hobbii Baby Snuggle is softest, and Premier Parfait Chunky is the near-interchangeable backup.
Cheapest quality acrylic is WeCrochet Brava (~1.1 cents/yd); cheapest Bernat route is Walmart multipacks -- but verify the listing price at checkout, they conflict.
Joann is gone (liquidated 2025). Practical channels now: Michaels, Hobby Lobby, Walmart, and direct online (Yarnspirations, Hobbii, Crochet.com).
Bulk paths: Yarnspirations has a formal wholesale program; 6060eyes.com (own site only, not Etsy) for safety eyes; Fairfield Poly-Fil 10lb boxes cheapest at Walmart.
Two watch-outs on the current yarn: Bernat dye-lot inconsistency plus a long discontinued-shades list, and chenille worming (mitigate with smaller hooks, tighter tension).

etsyFees.finding: Listing fee is $0.20 per listing, charged at creation and each 4-month renewal whether it sells or not.
Transaction fee is 6.5% of total order value including shipping/gift wrap; US payment processing (Etsy Payments) adds 3% + $0.25 per order.
Offsite Ads: 15% on ad-attributed orders if trailing-12-month sales are under $10,000 (can opt out); drops to 12% but becomes mandatory once you cross $10,000.
One-time shop setup fee of roughly $15-$29 for new shops (introduced Sept 2024). No US Regulatory Operating Fee exists (that fee applies only in certain countries, e.g. Canada 1.15%, UK 0.32%).
etsyFees.source: craftybase.com (2026; setup-fee range varies by source)

etsyFees.finding: Illustrative $25 plushie sale (free shipping, no offsite ad): $0.20 listing + $1.63 transaction + $1.00 processing = $2.83 (~11.3% all-in). If offsite-ad-attributed at 15%, add $3.75 for $6.58 total (~26.3%).
etsyFees.source: Arithmetic on verified 2026 rates; Etsy official fee page returned 403 so figures rest on consistent secondary sources

paymentProcessing.finding: Square: 2.6% + $0.15 per tap/dip/swipe on the free plan (raised from +$0.10 in the Oct 2025 pricing overhaul -- older sources showing 10 cents are outdated); contactless+chip reader $59; no monthly fee.
PayPal Zettle (now 'PayPal POS'): 2.29% + $0.09 in-person -- cheapest per-transaction card rate of the group; first reader $29 ($79 after); no monthly fee.
Venmo business profile: 1.9% + $0.10 on standard in-app QR payments -- cheapest option overall. Tap to Pay card rates conflict across sources (2.29% + $0.10 vs 2.9% + $0.09) -- verify in-app.
paymentProcessing.confidence: High (QR rate); Low (Tap to Pay rate)

paymentProcessing.finding: SumUp US: 2.6% + $0.10 in-person, reader ~$39-$54, no monthly fee (one craft-fair guide cites 2.75% -- US pricing pages vary).
Shopify POS is generally not worth it for a fair-only seller -- competitive in-person rates require a paid plan (~$128/month on Basic with POS Pro); only makes sense with an existing Shopify store.

Square is the most-used reader among handmade sellers per craft-fair guides (free app, easy setup, inventory tracking, next-day deposits); in practice most vendors offer Square/Zettle plus a Venmo QR code.

boothStartup.finding: Indoor artist-alley minimal kit (floor-length tablecloth, small risers, price signs, card reader) can be done for under ~$100 excluding banner; a vertical banner and gridwall panels are the usual first upgrades.

Consensus artist-alley checklist: floor-length table cover (hides storage), gridwall/wire displays for vertical space, large clear price signage, name banner, business cards, cash box, battery lighting.
Outdoor 10x10 pop-up canopy: budget models ~$80-$200, vendor-grade commercial frames $200-$400, custom-printed $400-$1,000+; weights add $50-$100.
Plan roughly 40lb of weight per canopy leg since staking is usually banned (some events require 25lb/leg); sidewalls are a recommended add-on for wind/sun control.
boothStartup.confidence: High (recommendation); the 40lb figure is one guide's rule of thumb

boothStartup.finding: Rough startup totals: indoor table budget setup ~$100-$250, mid-tier with banner + gridwall + lighting ~$300-$600; outdoor Ren-Faire booth budget ~$350-$600, mid-tier ~$800-$1,500. Ranges assembled from component prices, not a single sourced total.
Budget the booth fee itself at +20-30% over the headline fee for true event cost (parking, electricity, insurance riders).

pricingFormulas.finding: Formula A (most-cited for crochet): Price = (Materials + Time x Hourly Rate) x 2.0-2.5 markup.

Formula B (classic wholesale/retail): (Materials + Labor + Overhead) = base; base x2 = wholesale; wholesale x2 = retail (i.e. cost x4 retail). Overhead commonly estimated at 15-25% of materials + labor.
Formula C (Made Urban variant): (Materials x 2) + Labor + Overhead = wholesale, x2 = retail.
Hourly-rate benchmark corroborated: $15-25/hr general floor, $12-15 beginner, $15-25 intermediate, $25-40 advanced; amigurumi-specific guides use $20/hr in worked examples.

Known amigurumi tension: full formulas on slow-to-make plushies produce prices the market resists (a worked example prices an 8-hour elephant at $195). A $25 plushie only supports ~30-45 min of paid labor under Formula A -- guides recommend faster patterns or accepting some unpaid labor rather than lowering the hourly rate.

marketingChannels.finding: Hard, corroborated data comparing TikTok vs Instagram vs Etsy-search conversion for crochet plushie sellers specifically does not exist -- the evidence base is almost entirely anecdote.
marketingChannels.confidence: High (that this is the state of evidence)

marketingChannels.finding: Viral-TikTok anecdotes exist (2M+ views producing 400+ orders; 50k followers in 3 months leading to sell-out drops) but read like content-mill composites with no named/verifiable shops -- treat as illustrative only.

A genuine primary-source testimonial exists: a January 2026 YouTube '2025 Crochet Recap' where one plushie seller breaks down markets-vs-Etsy numbers (plushies sold, fees compared) -- worth watching directly.

Craft-business guides consistently report in-person craft fairs/markets as the strongest-converting channel for plushies (buyers can touch the item, no shipping friction), with Etsy as year-round baseline and social media as the discovery layer feeding both.
TikTok-to-Etsy crossover is observable: Etsy hosts dedicated 'viral TikTok crochet' market pages, indicating TikTok trends measurably drive Etsy search demand for plushies.

legal.finding: CDTFA seller's permit is required to sell taxable goods at CA conventions/craft fairs: a free temporary permit covers selling under 90 days, but doing 3+ events in 12 months requires a regular (permanent) permit -- also free. Obtain up to 90 days before the event via CDTFA online, registering each event location.
Event operators are required to verify vendor permits (typically via form CDTFA-410-D), and most convention vendor applications ask for your permit number.

Sales tax rate is the rate where the event is held: 7.25% statewide base plus district taxes (LA County venues run ~9.5%+). The vendor collects and remits on their own CDTFA return -- conventions do not remit for you. Use the CDTFA address-based rate lookup per venue.
legal.source: cdtfa.ca.gov district-tax page; taxjar.com festival guide

legal.finding: Liability insurance: Ren faires and larger conventions commonly require a certificate of insurance naming the event/venue as additional insured; small comic cons often do not. Typical craft-vendor cost: ACT Insurance from ~$49/event or ~$279/year; FLIP from ~$299/year (industry range $40-60/event, $200-400/year).

CPSIA: handmade plushies marketed to children 12-and-under are 'children's products' requiring third-party testing at a CPSC-accepted lab (ASTM F963), a Children's Product Certificate, and a permanent tracking label.

The CPSC Small Batch Manufacturer registry (free, annual; under ~$1.48M revenue and 7,500 units) waives most third-party testing but NOT lead-in-substrate rules -- and a CPC and tracking label are still required.

A 'not intended for children under 3' tag is NOT a reliable shield: CPSC classifies by overall design, marketing, and appeal -- a cute plushie displayed at a con will likely be deemed a children's product regardless of disclaimer. Adult/collector positioning only works if design and marketing genuinely target adults.
Several states require stuffed-article 'law tags'/registry numbers (e.g. Pennsylvania URN, honored by reciprocity in other states).

boothPresentation.finding: Build height variation with risers (crates, wooden blocks, acrylic stands, cake stands) rather than a flat table -- 'tall in back, medium middle, low front' is the most-repeated framing among craft-fair vendors.
Keep front booth corners low (~36in or under) so tall displays don't block sightlines into the booth from the aisle.
Amigurumi-specific: divide the table into zones by product type (dolls, animals, baby items) or by color gradient rather than mixing randomly, so shoppers can parse the offering at a glance.
boothPresentation.source: Crochet booth guide synthesis -- no single strong primary source

boothPresentation.finding: Placing a 'Fan Favorite' or 'Best Seller' sign next to your most detailed/popular plush, front and center, is a repeated crochet-specific tactic to anchor attention.
Mirrors placed under small items create an illusion of more product and add sparkle at near-zero cost -- borrowed from jewelry-vendor advice, not amigurumi-specific.
Visible, clearly marked individual price tags are near-universally recommended; hidden/ask-for-price setups are a direct sales blocker because most customers will not interrupt to ask.
Sign hierarchy: large store-name sign, medium price/custom-order signage, small payment-method/gift-certificate signs -- a tiered visual-priority system.

QR codes are used for more than payment: digital business cards, email-list opt-in, social growth, discount codes, care-instruction/tutorial links, and portfolio showcases of items not physically on the table.
Short, scannable signage phrasing ("locally sourced," "made to order," category labels) is recommended over paragraphs of text so passersby can parse a sign in a glance.

Live crocheting at the booth is repeatedly recommended: keeps the vendor visibly present-but-not-pushy, demonstrates authenticity/skill, produces new inventory during downtime, and starts conversations.

Prize/spinner wheels (discounts, small freebies, 'mystery' rewards) are a documented crowd-gathering tactic, prized for making the booth feel festive and drawing people from a distance -- sources are mostly commercially-motivated (game/display sellers), treat accordingly.
Building an email list at the booth is a top-tier tactic -- see the dedicated 'Email List Building & Usage' section below for how to capture it, which platform to use, and what to send.
boothPresentation.source: See Email List Building & Usage section

boothPresentation.finding: Physical punch cards for repeat con visits: not documented in vendor guides -- searches only surfaced generic loyalty-discount advice (10-15% off). Treat email/QR loyalty incentives as the closest sourced substitute.

Photo-op backdrops/props that get customers tagging the shop on social media: no vendor testimony or case study found on effectiveness -- only generic backdrop product listings. Appears to be an assumed-but-undocumented tactic.
boothPresentation.source: N/A -- no substantive sourced advice located

boothPresentation.finding: 'Shelfie' displays -- booth setups deliberately styled to be photogenic/pinnable using crate-and-shelf vertical arrangements -- are named as a current trend, though from a single general craft blog with no before/after data.

Pastel vs. dark/gothic booth aesthetic trends, and deliberate "squish-testing" sensory tactics, were not found documented anywhere as intentional booth strategies for 2024-2026 -- flag as unresearched, not "doesn't work."
Overcrowded tables overwhelm shoppers and cause people to walk past -- curate visible stock and store backup inventory out of sight underneath.
Flat, single-height tables read as "easy to walk past" -- lack of vertical depth is repeatedly cited as a top booth mistake.
Pricing everything in a single tier narrows the buyer segment; mixing impulse-buy price points ($5-15) with higher-ticket items is recommended instead.
Not accepting card/digital payment is called out as a direct lost-sales mistake at the booth level.

emailListBuilding.finding: QR code linking to an online form (Google Form, or an ESP's own signup page) is the most commonly recommended capture method for a one-person booth -- no staff needed, shopper self-serves on their own phone, works even after they've walked away.
Flodesk has a native QR-code generator built into its signup forms (Share -> QR code) that always points to the live, editable form -- no paper needed.

A clipboard/paper sheet is still viable and near-zero-cost, but illegible handwriting and the lag of manually retyping entries later is repeatedly flagged as the weakest option for a solo seller with no downtime to transcribe.

A tablet propped on the table running a free Google Form lets the shopper type their own entry directly into your system -- avoids both the transcription problem of paper and the "does the shopper have their phone out" friction of QR-only.

No dedicated third-party "booth email capture" app was found distinct from the email platforms' own form tools -- the practical stack is just your ESP's free form builder + a printed QR code, or a plain Google Form.
emailListBuilding.source: Research synthesis -- no specific app found

emailListBuilding.finding: Keep the signup form to name + email (or just email) only -- every additional field measurably drops signup conversion at a booth.

MailerLite is repeatedly named the best free-tier option for small sellers: free plan covers up to 1,000 subscribers with real automations, forms, and landing pages included (12,000 emails/month under ~500 subscribers).

Mailchimp's free tier was cut back for 2026 to only 250 contacts and 500 sends/month (down from 500 contacts/2,500 sends), with sending held once you exceed 250 contacts and no scheduled campaigns on free -- weak for anyone actively growing a list.

Flodesk is genuinely popular specifically among Etsy/handmade sellers for its design aesthetic (warm, artisanal templates) and flat-rate pricing (~$38/mo unlimited contacts), but its free tier only builds forms -- no actual sends without a paid plan.

Klaviyo and ConvertKit(Kit) are generally described as overkill for a small solo crafter -- Klaviyo is built for serious e-commerce automation, Kit is creator/course-focused; both add complexity a booth-level list doesn't need yet.

Bottom line for a solo crochet seller starting out: MailerLite (best free functionality) or Flodesk (best design fit for a handmade brand, but paid) are the two "right-sized" names; Mailchimp's shrunken free tier and Klaviyo's e-commerce complexity are the two most commonly flagged as poor fits.
Recommended send cadence for a small seasonal handmade business: roughly monthly, or quarterly for highly seasonal product lines, ramping to 2-3x/month around holidays/peak selling season.

Content mix leans non-promotional/interest-based rather than pure sales pitches: seasonal/style inspiration, gift-guide content, and behind-the-scenes process content, with product drops/restocks/discount codes woven in rather than being the whole email.

General small-list/niche newsletter open rates run roughly 17-28%, with arts/hobbies niches on the higher end (~27%); pure promotional/restock sends tend to run lower (~15-20%). No handmade/crochet-specific benchmark was found -- these are general email-industry figures.
Etsy has no built-in mass-email/marketing tool for sellers to message past buyers -- Shop Manager does not include a bulk-email feature.

Etsy policy explicitly bars adding any Etsy buyer to an external email or physical mailing list without that buyer's separate consent -- a sale on Etsy does not automatically grant permission to email them.
emailListBuilding.source: Etsy seller policy, quoted via marketsy.io; optinmonster.com

emailListBuilding.finding: Practical implication: your booth-collected list and your Etsy customer base must stay separate, non-overlapping pools unless a buyer independently opts in (e.g. a link in packaging or a thank-you note) -- third-party tools exist to request that opt-in, but none let you skip consent.
emailListBuilding.source: Direct consequence of Etsy policy above

emailListBuilding.finding: CAN-SPAM does not legally require prior opt-in consent to add someone to a list, but every commercial email must include a clear, working unsubscribe mechanism, honored within 10 business days, free and low-friction (no fee, no extra personal info required beyond email).

Practical minimum for a solo crafter's booth list: get an affirmative signup (person writes/types their own email, ideally with a stated 'sign up for emails' line) -- de facto best practice and also required by every ESP's terms of service to keep a sending account in good standing.
emailListBuilding.source: Synthesized from FTC guide + standard ESP terms

emailListBuilding.finding: MailerLite -- the platform recommended above as the best free-tier fit -- does not have a native built-in QR code generator for its signup forms as of 2026. Pairing it with a free third-party QR tool is required to get a scannable code for the booth.
emailListBuilding.source: qrcode-tiger.com; appypieautomate.ai; viasocket.com (absence confirmed via third-party-integration listings, not an explicit MailerLite denial)

emailListBuilding.finding: Mailchimp's own signup-form creation flow includes a native QR code sharing option alongside link/Facebook/Twitter -- notable since Mailchimp was otherwise flagged above as a weaker fit due to its shrunken 2026 free tier.

Regardless of which ESP is used, any signup-form URL can be turned into a QR code for free with a generic tool (QRCodeChimp, the-qrcode-generator.com, ME-QR, QRStuff) -- paste the form link in, download the QR image, print it for the booth. No account or cost required.

Watch for the wrong QR type: an 'email QR code' generator typically encodes a mailto: link that pre-fills a compose window addressed to the SELLER's email, which does not collect the shopper's address. The QR must encode the signup FORM's URL instead, so scanning opens the form and the shopper enters their own email.
emailListBuilding.source: Direct consequence of how mailto: vs. URL QR codes function

atAGlance: Before the first table: get the free CDTFA seller's permit (required, and events verify it) and budget ~$49/event or ~$279/yr for vendor insurance where required.
CPSIA is the sleeper risk: cute plushies sold at cons likely count as children's products -- register free as a CPSC Small Batch Manufacturer; an 'under 3' disclaimer does not exempt you.
Pricing math: (Materials + Time x $15-25/hr) x 2-2.5 markup, mixing $5-15 impulse tiers with bigger pieces -- and know that a $25 plushie only supports ~30-45 min of paid labor.
At the booth: take cards (Square 2.6% + 15 cents is the default), show visible prices, and build vertical displays -- the three highest-confidence rules found.
Online: Etsy runs ~11.3% all-in on a $25 sale; build an owned email list via QR-to-form (MailerLite free tier) -- but Etsy buyers legally cannot be auto-added to it.
